title: Investigating “Who Is Reciting the Buddha”: Answers to a Guest's Questions
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: It is said that Master Yinguang opposed investigative recitation. Why, then, do you discuss “investigating who is reciting the Buddha” in the article Investigative Recitation of the Buddha's Name?

inline.s: Question: It is said that Master Yinguang opposed investigative recitation. Why, then, do you discuss “investigating who is reciting the Buddha” in the article
Investigative Recitation of the Buddha's Name
Answer: In receiving and guiding students, the patriarchs gave medicine according to the illness (prescribed medicine according to the illness).

For example, the Dream Wanderings Collection records that Master Hanshan Deqing taught some students to contemplate the mind, some to investigate Chan, some to recite the Buddha's name, and some to uphold mantras — all according to the specific circumstances of the person concerned. Therefore one may not use one instruction to negate another, still less take certain instructions that were given according to a person's particular circumstances and present them as the patriarch's teaching for all people.
Master Yinguang did not oppose investigative recitation; rather, he was cautioning those who lack a foundation, or who do not value faith and vows.

[Lack a foundation] Lacking a foundation is not something fixed and unchanging. If you know you lack a foundation, then follow the chapter “The Preliminaries” in this article to build it up, and you will have a foundation. In practice, examples of latecomers who surpass their predecessors and rise to distinction are seen again and again. The key is to work hard — and to know how to work hard.

And for Pure Land students who already have a foundation and whose faith and vows are both complete, Master Yinguang, in his Record of Groping for the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, explains in detail how to carry out investigative recitation. For example:
One must, upon this
(the word “zhe,” i.e., “this”)
single thought of ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha,’
investigate it again and again
, and stir it up earnestly.”
He also explains in detail the state of attainment and the benefits of investigative recitation:

“As for its benefits: in the present, while not yet leaving Sahā, one constantly joins the assembly of the lotus pool; at life's end, one ascends at once to the highest grade and instantly realizes the Buddha-vehicle.”

(In translation: as for the benefits of attaining the Buddha-recitation samādhi — in the present, though one has not yet left the Sahā world, one constantly joins the lotus-pool assembly of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; at the end of life, one immediately ascends to the highest grade and is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and upon arriving there instantly realizes the Buddha-vehicle.)

Master Yinguang (the thirteenth patriarch of the Pure Land school) worried that discussing investigative recitation in the Record of Groping for the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi would provoke the controversy “Is it Chan? Is it Pure Land?” So in that work he particularly admonished with earnest gravity:
Do not speak of it to those outside the gate.
For only when one's state has reached that stage does one know its perfect interpenetration and ultimacy. Master Yinguang said:
“Only those within the household know the household's affairs; speak of it to those outside the gate, and slander is sure to follow.”
(For details, see
Master Yinguang's
Record of Groping for the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi
[Speak of it to those outside the gate, and slander is sure to follow] Although Master Yongming, who was Amitābha Buddha come again, had long ago taught:
“With Chan and with Pure Land both, one is like a tiger with horns — a teacher of humans in this life, a Buddha or patriarch in the next.”
there are still not a few Pure Land practitioners who turn pale at the mention of Chan. So deep is this prejudice, and of such long standing, that even Master Yinguang sighed:
“Slander is sure to follow!”
In fact, whether a practice is Pure Land practice hinges on whether faith and vows are complete. Master Ouyi (the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
“A Chan practitioner who wishes to be born in the West need not switch to reciting the Buddha's name; if he simply possesses faith and vows, then his Chan investigation is itself Pure Land practice.”
(Master Ouyi's Pure Land Collection,
“Occasional Talks in the Brahma Room.”)
Moreover, the condition for rebirth is: at life's end, ten thoughts in continuity (see
The Conditions for Rebirth

for details). For a Buddha-rectiter whose faith and vows are complete, it is only natural to recite in whatever way makes it easy to achieve thought-after-thought continuity, and even the undisturbed one-pointed mind. Whether to recite straight on or to practice investigative recitation, each person should choose according to his or her own circumstances.
Therefore Master Lianchi (
the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school
) taught: “
Dufeng and Tianqi both taught investigative recitation of the Buddha's name; why then did Konggu say
one need not use these methods
It is because they differed according to the person's capacity

for some people, investigation suits their capacity and has real effect, so they may adopt investigative recitation; for others, reciting straight on has real effect, so there is no need to investigate — it is enough just to recite ordinarily
, each being free and unobstructed
(each following what suits them)
” (Encouragement to Advance Through the Chan Barrier)
Master Lianchi
also said:
“In our dynasty
(meaning the present dynasty)
, during the Hongwu and Yongle periods
(the Hongwu and Yongle reign periods)

, there were the three great elders Konggu, Tianqi, and Dufeng. On reciting the Buddha's name, the two masters Tian and Du both taught people to contemplate ‘who is reciting the Buddha?,’ while Konggu alone said ‘just recite straight on, and there is also a gate of awakening.’ These two
(reciting straight on and investigation)
each suit different capacities, and both are correct
(both are right)
. And Konggu only said that reciting straight on is also acceptable
(that is, Konggu only said that straight recitation is also possible)
he did not say that investigation is wrong
(he did not say that investigation is mistaken)
The Bamboo Window, Second Collection
Master Ouyi's Treatise on Investigative Recitation of the Buddha's Name says:

“Question: With the Pure Land as one's main practice, can investigation take the place of reciting the Buddha's name? Answer: Both investigation and recitation belong to the category of practice; if one is earnest, then investigation also leads to rebirth
(if one is diligent, investigation also leads to rebirth)
, and if one is not earnest, then recitation also does not lead to rebirth
(if one is not diligent, even straight recitation cannot lead to rebirth)
. Furthermore, even if there is earnest practice, if it is guided by faith and vows, one is reborn; without the guidance of faith and vows, one is not reborn.”
This is to say: for those who practice the Pure Land, straight recitation can lead to rebirth, and investigation can also lead to rebirth; the key is diligence together with complete faith and vows.

Therefore, if you yourself feel that reciting straight on is good, then recite straight on, and do not denigrate investigative recitation; if you yourself feel that investigative recitation is good, then practice investigative recitation, and do not denigrate reciting straight on.
Question: Are investigative recitation and embodying investigation one or two?

Answer: The two are one; embodying investigation is investigative recitation. In his teachings, Master Lianchi used both the term “investigation” (canjiu) and the term “embodying investigation” (tijiu). For example:
In The Yunqi Collection, Master Lianchi said:
“Now, ‘the one who recites the Buddha's name’ — that is, upon the recitation of the Buddha's name, to
investigate
’ — is still one gate, not two matters. If
investigation
is inconvenient, then reciting straight on is also acceptable.”
He also said:
“Question: Chan investigation values the non-arising of a single thought, while reciting the Buddha's name values the continuation of pure thoughts. Now this
investigative recitation
is a single gate, its intent being wondrous awakening and thereby attaining rebirth.”
He also said:

Truly, if you can see through this very single thought of Buddha-recitation the moment it arises, rest assured that the great matter is settled. Yet you must not, upon seeing these words, begin to speculate and conjecture, straining for an understanding — for then you will lose it instead. Simply, thought after thought,
embody-investigate
, and with genuine accumulation and long effort you will attain it of yourself; only this is true awakening.

(In translation: In truth, as long as one can see through this single thought of Buddha-recitation the moment it arises, the great matter of illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature is assuredly settled. But one must not, upon seeing my saying “if you can see through this single thought of Buddha-recitation the moment it arises, rest assured the great matter is settled,” go on to speculate and conjecture about its meaning, straining far-fetched interpretations to seek comprehension. If one does so, one loses the true intent. Just wholeheartedly, in the state of no-thought, embody and investigate; with genuine work and accumulated effort, after a long time you will attain it of yourself. Only this is true awakening.)
[Speculate and conjecture (sibu
bǔ
duo)] To speculate and conjecture. [Straining for understanding] To force far-fetched interpretations in order to seek comprehension.
He also said:
Embody-investigation

means that on hearing the Buddha's name, one does not merely recall it, but turns the recitation back to contemplate, examining to the utmost and tracing it to its root. When this embody-investigation reaches its limit, it suddenly accords with one's own original mind.”
He also said:

“Suffering arises from the body, the body arises from karma, and so on. Illness is one of the sufferings, and its roundabout mutual causation is likewise. One should, diligently and minutely, by day and night,
embody-investigate

. If investigation yields nothing, simply raise the phrase of the primary investigative recitation — the Buddha's name — and turn the light back to look at yourself. When you recognize where this thought settles, the delusion breaks of itself. When the delusion breaks, they dissolve in turn, and so it is likewise.”

(In translation: suffering arises from the body, the body from karma, karma from delusion, and so on. Illness is one of the sufferings, so it too is delusion, karma, body, and suffering arising in mutual succession. One should diligently (zizi) and minutely (mimi), by day and night, embody-investigate. If the investigation yields nothing, simply raise the primary investigative phrase of Buddha-recitation (the Buddha's name) and turn the light back to look within: Who is reciting the Buddha? When you recognize where this thought settles, the delusion breaks of itself. When the delusion breaks, the karma breaks; when the karma breaks, the body breaks; when the body breaks, the suffering (illness) breaks — thus they dissolve in succession.)
In the Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra, Master Lianchi said:
“To recall and recollect without interruption is called holding in practice; to
embody-investigate

without interruption is called holding in principle. These shall be discussed in detail below and taken as the cause. The one-pointed mind that comes later also has its practice aspect and its principle aspect. Those who do not understand this think that reciting the Buddha's name is only for those of dull faculties and that only investigating Chan can bring awakening. Beginners who hear this cannot decide for themselves. They do not know that
embody-investigative recitation

is extremely close in meaning to the way the worthy elders of former generations taught people to raise a huatou and cultivate the sensation of doubt. Hence it is said that in investigating Chan one need not raise a separate huatou; it is enough to apply oneself to the single phrase ‘Amitābha Buddha.’ How wonderful are these words!”
In The Bamboo Window, Second Collection, Master Lianchi has a chapter devoted to “
investigative recitation
,” in which he says:
In our dynasty
the present dynasty
, during the Hongwu and Yongle periods
the Hongwu and Yongle reign periods

, there were the three great elders Konggu, Tianqi, and Dufeng. On reciting the Buddha's name, the two masters Tian and Du both taught people to contemplate “who is reciting the Buddha?,” while Konggu alone said that simply reciting straight on also has a gate of awakening.
